dataset: Pipe materials for an ASTM C680-style insulated-pipe simulator: PVC (ASTM D1785 Sch 40/80) and CPVC (F441) dimensions, conductivity and temperature limits; copper tube (ASTM B88 K/L/M, DWV, ACR B280) walls and conductivity; C585 copper insulation additions; how 3E Plus / C680 / NIA MIDG / ORNL MEASUR treat the pipe wall

conventions.unverified: The literal string 'unverified' (and each entry of the top-level 'unverified' list) means no fetched source stated the value. Nothing was guessed, averaged, interpolated, converted between unit systems, or filled from memory.
conventions.src: Every value or statement carries 'src', a list of ids in this file's top-level 'sources' array (G1-G20), plus a 'location' (page, table or code line).
conventions.quotes: 'quote' strings are verbatim from pdftotext output (-layout, -raw or default), HTML-to-text, or JavaScript source. Line breaks and hyphenation splits were joined and runs of spaces collapsed; nothing else was changed. Table cells are joined with ' | ' where a quote spans cells.
conventions.quote_check: The build script searched every quote not read from an image in the saved text of its cited source (Unicode NFKC, whitespace, '|' and hyphenated line breaks ignored; curly quotes folded to straight). 'quote_check' records the result. Quotes read visually from a screenshot say so.
conventions.printed_rows: Table rows were parsed programmatically from pdftotext output. Each row keeps 'printed'/'printed_row'/'printed_line': the source line with runs of spaces collapsed, so every number can be traced. Unicode fraction glyphs in nominal sizes were rewritten as '1-1/4' style strings; the printed text is kept alongside. Charlotte rows come from pdftotext -raw, where a split fraction such as '1' + '⁄4”' was rejoined, so '11⁄4”' in a printed string means 1-1/4.
conventions.consensus_fields: In the PVC tables, 'od_in', 'min_wall_in' and 'avg_id_in' at row level are filled only when every source that prints that cell gives the identical number; otherwise they read 'sources disagree (see by_source)'. No value was averaged or chosen.
conventions.agent_checks: Keys starting 'agent_check' and the 'agent_consistency_checks' blocks are arithmetic done by the research agent on sourced numbers (for example OD - 2 x wall vs printed ID). They are cross-checks, not source values.

units.k_inch_pound: as printed by each source; Btu*in/(h*ft2*F) unless the quote says otherwise (CDA G2 prints Btu/ sq ft/ ft hr/ F, i.e. a per-foot thickness basis)
units.r_value: Charlotte (G3) prints R = wall thickness / C with C in BTU in/Hr Sq Ft F, so R is in h*ft2*F/Btu per square foot of wall (a flat-wall figure; G3 does not state units on the R table itself)

manufacturer.quote: CPVC and PVC pipe have a much lower thermal conductivity factor than metal pipe. Therefore, fluids being piped maintain a more constant temperature. In many cases, pipe insulation is not required.
Due to its low coefficient of thermal conductivity, it is often not necessary to insulate FlowGuard Gold CPVC against condensation within conditioned buildings.

Two conditions that control sweating of a pipe are (1) the pipe surface temperature, which depends on the temperature of the water inside the pipe and (2) the relative humidity of the air around the pipe. Because each of the factors can vary greatly, it is possible that conditions exist that can cause CPVC pipe to sweat.
Under most conditions that cause copper pipe to sweat and drip, FlowGuard Gold pipe will remain free of condensation.
Note: Always follow local code requirements for insulation installation. Some code jurisdictions require insulation to be installed in accordance with the International Energy Conservation Code.

All model plumbing codes require that piping exposed to freezing temperatures be properly insulated.

With a dramatically lower thermal conductivity factor as compared to metal, thermoplastic systems have less heat loss or gain, and sustain the temperature of the service with less variation than metal piping. As a result, pipe insulation is often not required.

Compared with traditional pipe materials, the thermal conductivity of vinyl is low and it essentially acts as an insulator. This insulating property provides a distinct advantage over traditional materials to prevent “sweating” or formation of condensation on the pipe wall. The need for insulation may, in certain instances, be completely eliminated by using vinyl for cold or chilled water lines.
The graph shown in Figure 7 gives an example of the extent to which vinyl piping products will prevent the formation of condensation at different temperatures of the process fluid.

nia_midg_calculators.how_it_works: r_thickness = (D_outer/2) ln(pipe_od/pipe_id), where D_outer is the insulation OD (or pipe OD when bare), so the wall resistance is referred to the outer surface area like the insulation term (r_effective_thickness uses the same D_outer/2 factor). Units follow from inches / (Btu*in/(h*ft2*F)) = h*ft2*F/Btu (agent reading; the code states no units).

plastic_pipe_formula_ipex.formula_as_printed: q = [π x L x (Do – Di)] / ln(Do/Di) x K x Δt / (ro – ri)
plastic_pipe_formula_ipex.formula_source: read from a rendered image of IPEX p. 34 (the equation is typeset; pdftotext scrambles it)

symbols_quote.quote: Do = Average outside diameter, ft Di = Average inside diameter, ft ro = Average outside radius, in. ri = Average inside radius, in.

caveat_quote.quote: Note that in more complex situations, heat loss or gain should be calculated taking into account such things as heat transfer coefficients, fluid conductivity, fluid heat capacity, viscosity, air temperature and air velocity.

plastic_pipe_formula_ipex.agent_reading: Wall conduction only: log-mean area x K x dT / wall thickness. With Do, Di in ft and ro, ri in in., it reduces to q = 2*pi*(K/12)*L*dT/ln(Do/Di) Btu/h for K in Btu*in/(h*ft2*F), the standard cylindrical-wall formula. Delta-t is across the wall, not fluid-to-air.

example_values_from_ipex.quote: For example, copper, a good conductor of heat, will lose 2700 BTU per hour per square foot of surface area with a wall thickness of 1” while vinyl will lose only 1.2 BTU/hr.
Note that if the vinyl wall thickness is reduced to 0.25 inches, the heat loss increases four times.

summary_for_simulator: Pipe material enters the published tools in two ways: (1) bare-surface emittance (3E Plus base metal list, MIDG/DNV emissivity) and (2) wall conduction, which the NIA MIDG code (steel only), ORNL MEASUR (user k) and the IPEX plastic formula include as a cylindrical term. 3E Plus v4.1 and C680 public text do not say whether the wall term is used.
Sourced inputs for a wall term: PVC k 1.2 or 1.02 and CPVC k 0.95-0.96 Btu*in/(h*ft2*F) (C177); copper C12200 k 196 Btu*ft/(h*ft2*F) at 68 F; OD/min-wall (PVC) and OD/ID/wall (copper) tables above.
